summary: German has three imperative forms, one for each way of saying “you”. To one person you say du to: the stem, often without an ending – Geh! Komm! Warte! (Gehe! with -e is correct but formal or old-fashioned; after -t / -d the -e is needed: Warte!). To several people you say ihr to: the ihr form of the present without ihr – Geht! Kommt! Wartet! To one or more people you say Sie to: the infinitive form + Sie, verb first – Gehen Sie! Kommen Sie! Warten Sie! (the pronoun is never left out). The verb stands first and the sentence ends with an exclamation mark. Verbs that change e to i / ie in the present keep it and drop the -e: essen → Iss! (du isst), nehmen → Nimm!, lesen → Lies!; verbs that change a to ä do NOT keep the umlaut: fahren → Fahr! (du fährst), laufen → Lauf! (du läufst). A separable particle goes to the end: Komm herein! Geh weg! Kommen Sie bitte zurück! sein is irregular: Sei …! Seid …! Seien Sie …! bitte (please), mal and doch make a command softer: Komm doch mal her! – and nicht makes it negative: Geh nicht weg! “Let’s …” is the wir form with the verb first: Gehen wir! Signs and recipes often use the bare infinitive: Bitte nicht rauchen! Langsam fahren!

blocks.caption: The du form: the present without du and without -st (du isst → Iss!, but du fährst → Fahr!)

blocks.title: Who are you talking to?
blocks.text: One friend → Komm! · several friends → Kommt! · anyone you call Sie (one or many) → Kommen Sie!

blocks.title: No umlaut, but keep the i
blocks.text: Fahr! Lauf! (not *Fähr!, *Läuf!) – but Iss! Nimm! Lies! (the i stays).

blocks.title: Never drop Sie
blocks.text: Kommen Sie! – Kommen! alone is not a polite command (a bare infinitive sounds like a sign or a drill instruction).

blocks.title: Softeners
blocks.text: bitte (please), mal, doch: Warte bitte! · Komm mal her! · Bleib doch hier! – without them a German command can sound sharp.

blocks.title: Separable verbs
blocks.text: The particle closes the command: Komm herein! Geh weg! Kommen Sie bitte zurück!

German has a separate polite form with the pronoun: Gehen Sie!

askYourself: Who am I talking to: one person I say du to, several people I say ihr to, or someone I say Sie to?
du: take the du form of the present, drop du and -st: du kommst → Komm!
Does the verb change e → i / ie (essen, nehmen, lesen)? Keep the i: Iss! – Does it change a → ä (fahren, laufen)? Drop the umlaut: Fahr!
Does the stem end in -t or -d (warten, finden)? Add -e: Warte!
ihr: the ihr form of the present, without ihr: Kommt!
Sie: the infinitive form + Sie, verb first: Kommen Sie!
Separable verb? Put the particle at the end: Komm herein!
Is it sein? Sei! – Seid! – Seien Sie!
Do I want to sound friendly? Add bitte, mal or doch; to forbid, add nicht.
steps: Verb first, the rest after, a separable particle last.

traps: Fahr! and Lauf! have no umlaut (du fährst, du läufst).
Iss! Nimm! Lies! keep the i of du isst, du nimmst, du liest – and take no -e.
The Sie form keeps Sie: Warten Sie bitte! – not *Warten bitte!
Warte! needs the -e (stem in -t); Geh! / Gehe! both work.
sein: Sei ruhig! (du), Seid ruhig! (ihr), Seien Sie ruhig! (Sie) – not *Bist ruhig!
The particle goes last: Komm herein! – not *Hereinkomm!
Negative: nicht after the verb (and its object): Geh nicht! Iss das nicht!

quiz.why: a → ä verbs lose the umlaut in the imperative: du fährst → Fahr!
e → i verbs keep the i and drop the ending: du isst → Iss!
Sie form = infinitive form + Sie, verb first.
ihr form = ihr kommt without ihr; the particle herein goes last.

quiz.q: sein – Sie form: “Please be on time!”

quiz.why: Stem in -t: the -e is needed in standard German (Wart! is only colloquial).

seeAlso.note: Arabic changes the imperative for a man, a woman and a group (اُكْتُبْ / اُكْتُبِي / اُكْتُبُوا); a negative command is لَا + the jussive (لَا تَكْتُبْ) – German changes it for du / ihr / Sie.
Hebrew לֵךְ / לְכִי / לְכוּ (to a man / a woman / several); everyday speech often uses the future as a softer command, and “don’t” is אַל + future.
Chinese verbs do not change: 来！ 走！; 请 + verb is polite, 别 / 不要 + verb is “don’t”, and 吧 softens – German needs a different verb form for du, ihr and Sie.
The du and ihr imperatives are built from the present forms (du kommst → Komm!, ihr kommt → Kommt!).
du / ihr / Sie: the same choice of address decides the imperative.
